list.listitem: Examine closely any asymptomatic flesh-colored, pink, red, or blue lesion that a patient states is changing in size, shape, symptoms (itching, tenderness) and is growing rapidly on sun-exposed skin. B
Perform a full-thickness excisional skin biopsy for pathological study to diagnose Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC). B
Early detection and clinician recognition of this disease may improve survival. B

background.definition: MCC is an uncommon and aggressive cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma. It arises in the dermis but can involve epidermis and deeper structures. Tumor cells have a propensity to spread to regional lymph nodes and distant sites.

list.listitem: The estimated annual incidence is 3 persons per million in the United States.
The incidence of MCC has increased threefold over the past 20 years.
Approximately 1500 new cases of MCC were diagnosed in the United States in 2008.
A Japanese series found that the incidence was lower in the US with an average age of 77 years and not difference in incidence by sex.
The incidence of MCC is increased approximately 11-fold for people with AIDS and fivefold for people who have undergone an organ transplant.

Risk factors that likely contribute to the etiology of MCC are: History of extensive ultraviolet radiation exposure. Advancing age. Fair skin. The higher risk among people of European ancestry may be related to a deficiency of protective melanin. The majority of tumors appear on the face and head, and many patients have other sun-associated skin cancers. Immunosuppression. Increased incidence in people with HIV/AIDS, organ transplantation, cell-mediated immune deficiencies, and other neoplasms. Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV), which is present in the majority of MCC tissue specimens and strongly underlines its possible role as an etiologic agent. In a review of over 38,000 cases of MCC in the US 65% were attributed to UV radiation exposure and 64% were associated with Merkel cell polyomavirus, with only a small proportion attributed to immunesuppressive conditions.

The role of ultraviolet rays in the development of MCC appears to be immunosuppressive (eg, by induction of immunosuppressive cytokines such as interleukin-10) rather than mutagenic; there is a striking epidemiologic association between immunosuppression and MCC.
Human MCPyV is frequently found in MCC tissue and it is believed to be causally linked to its pathogenesis.

Suspect MCC in patients with a flesh-colored, pink, red, or blue lesion that a patient states is changing in size, shape, and symptoms (itching, tenderness) and is growing rapidly on sun-exposed skin (especially if patient is immunosuppressed). B
Perform a full-thickness excisional skin biopsy for pathological study to diagnose MCC. B
Sentinel lymph node biopsies are recommended routinely for patients with MCC. B
Consider further workup for immunosuppression. C

MCC usually presents as a bland, painless, red, pink, blue, or violaceous nodule or cyst on sun-exposed skin areas; it is more common in white elderly people and those with a history of immunosuppression. Lesions are usually non-tender.
In a Japanese review, 63% of lesions were on the head and neck, 15% lower limb, 13% upper limb, 5% trunk, 4% buttocks, and 1% genitals.

MCC lesions are usually initially thought to be a cyst or some other lesion (such as pyogenic granuloma, scar, chalazion, epidermoid cyst, neurofibroma, or amelanotic melanoma). In a study of 195 patients, a cyst or acneiform lesion was the single most common presumptive diagnosis (32%), followed by lipoma (6%), dermatofibroma or fibroma (4%), and vascular lesion (4%). Malignant diagnoses comprised an additional 36%, with nonmelanoma skin cancer being the most common of these (19%), followed by lymphoma (6%), metastatic carcinoma (2%), and sarcoma (2%). The correct clinical diagnosis of MCC was made presumptively in only 1% of the cases.
Most of the lesions are asymptomatic but the majority of patients report rapid growth of their tumor within 3 months.
The most common anatomic sites of the lesion are the head and neck, followed by the lower and upper extremities.
Use good light and magnification to examine suspicious lesions, or use a dermatoscope if available. Previous photos of the lesion can be very helpful.
Examine lymph nodes to evaluate lymph node enlargement.
Dermatopathology study of a full-thickness excisional skin biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing MCC.
Immunohistochemistry is used to distinguish MCC from morphologically similar malignancies, including some lymphomas, Ewing sarcoma, and especially small-cell carcinoma of the lung.
Malignant MCC cells typically stain for cytokeratin 20 (CK20), which is a useful criterion for the diagnosis of MCC and improves its recognition.
MCPyV has been shown to be absent from other cutaneous neoplasms. It is a specific marker for MCC that helps in distinguishing cases of metastatic MCC from other high-grade neuroendocrine tumors.
Sentinel lymph node biopsies are recommended.
Initiate a metastatic workup with imaging if the lymph node is positive for MCC.
Consider further workup for immunosuppression (eg, HIV disease) in patients diagnosed with MCC.

A risk score was developed in a cohort of 618 patients, but has not been externally validated. I provides likelihood of recurrence based on time since diagnosis, stage, site, immune suppression, age and sex. It is available as an online calculator.
MCC is seldom suspected at presentation. Suspect MCC in a lesion on an extremity that is changing in size, shape, color, and is growing rapidly. See for a useful mnemonic.
Examine the lymph nodes to evaluate for lymph node enlargement.
Perform a biopsy of all suspicious lesions to confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment generally involves combinations of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.
Stage-specific treatment regimens have been outlined involving various combinations of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy for stage I to III disease. B
The emphasis of treatment of patients with stage IV disease is on palliative care with or without radiotherapy or chemotherapy. B
First-line treatment should involve surgical excision with pathologic verification of complete removal of the tumor.

Moh's micrographic surgery has been compared with wide local excision of the tumour in retrospective analyses of population databases with mixed results as to which gives better outcome. These studies are subject to selection bias as these have not been randomised trials.

Data from case series and meta-analyses of case series suggest that surgery in combination with adjuvant radiotherapy confer significant benefits with regard to reducing local and regional recurrence rates and prolonging disease-free survival in patients with Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) compared with surgery alone.

A systematic review identified 29 studies (both prospective trials and retrospective series) comparing patients receiving and not receiving adjuvant radiotherapy. Adjuvant radiotherapy was associated with better overall survival and disease-free survival. Earlier stage disease, shorter follow-up duration, size >2 cm, and being younger were associated with better overall survival.

A trial of adjuvant nivolumab versus observation following surgical resection of MCC suggests a disease-free survival benefit with immunotherapy (84% versus 73% disease free at 2 years). However, this was at the expense of increased adverse events and overall survival results are not mature.
There are retrospective case series suggesting a possible role for definitive radiotherapy in patients unsuitable for surgery.

While sentinel lymph node biopsy is usually recommended for staging. An observational study of 150 patients at the Mayo Clinic found disease specific survival rates of 97%, 82% and 82% at 1, 3 and 5 years respectively if the patient had a positive sentinal lymph node biopsy, and 99%, 95% and 87% if it was negative.
Systemic chemotherapy together with radiotherapy should be recommended for MCC if there is recurrent or disseminated disease.

A systematic review identified little data on the best chemotherapy for patients with metastatic MCC. They report response rates of 53% to 61% for first-line chemotherapy and 23% to 45% for second-line chemotherapy. However, the duration of any response was less than 8 months.

A small randomised phase 2 trial of combination immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab with or without stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) demonstrated no benefit from addition of SBRT but a very high overall response rate in advanced Merkel cell cancer to combination immunotherapy. In the checkpoint inhibitor naive group the response rate was 100%, and even as second line the combination provided 31% response rate.
The emphasis of treatment of patients with stage IV disease is on palliative care with or without radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

MCC prognosis is highly associated with the extent of disease at presentation. It is strongly related to the presence or absence of tumor in regional lymph nodes and prognosis is poor with distant metastasis. B

A risk score was developed in a cohort of 618 patients, but has not been externally validated. I provides likelihood of recurrence based on time since diagnosis, stage, site, immune suppression, age and sex. It is available as an online calculator. B
Both the presence of nodal involvement and the number of nodes involved are predictive of survival and even in small tumours it is recommended that evaluation of the nodes in undertaken.
The disease course is difficult to predict and ranges from relatively indolent to highly aggressive, often spreading to local, regional, and distant sites. B
In addition to skin cancers, patients with MCC have an increased risk for chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and other cancers. B
Recurrence is common, and 5-year survival ranges from 23% to 80% in different series. Recurrence is more common among patients seropositive for Merkel cell polyomavirus antibodies.

An observational study of 150 patients at the Mayo Clinic found disease specific survival rates of 97%, 82% and 82% at 1, 3 and 5 years respectively if the patient had a positive sentinal lymph node biopsy, and 99%, 95% and 87% if it was negative.
p63 expression is associated with higher mortality (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.7-5.1) based on a systematic review of case series and case reports.

Surgery is often not possible in elderly patients with multiple comorbidities and in patients with advanced lesions. Definitive radiotherapy should therefore be recommended as an option for these patients.

feature.caption: Mnemonic of MCC Risk Factors: AEIOU.
feature.feature_body:
A Asymptomatic or lack of tenderness
E Expanding rapidly
I Immunosuppression
O Older than 50 years
U Ultraviolet radiation–exposed site
From Heath M, Jaimes N, Lemos B, et al. Clinical characteristics of Merkel cell carcinoma at diagnosis in 195 patients: the AEIOU features. J Am Acad Dermatol 2008;58:375–381.
